extracted.intended_audience: federal litigators and judges (patent/infringement counsel and parties in federal district court)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and contract-interpretation rules used to decide whether plaintiffs in a patent-related suit had Article III standing and whether contractual assignment/control of litigation rights deprived them of the ability to sue. Focuses on summary-judgment and contract-construction principles in federal court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary judgment is appropriate when the evidence, viewed in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party, presents no genuine issue of material fact. (Fed. R. Civ. P. 56; Celotex Corp. v. Catrett; Anderson v. Liberty Lobby.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opposing party may not rest on pleadings but must produce significant probative evidence demonstrating a genuine issue for trial. The mere existence of some alleged factual dispute will not defeat a properly supported motion; the requirement is that there be no genuine issue of material fact. Use this rule to evaluate motions for summary judgment and determine whether factual disputes are material and supported by probative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of establishing Article III standing
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of establishing Article III standing always lies with the party invoking federal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To sustain the burden a plaintiff must prove a 'personal injury fairly traceable to the defendant’s allegedly unlawful conduct and likely to be redressed by the requested relief.' (Dep’t of Commerce v. U.S. House of Representatives.) Courts must assess whether the plaintiff has produced evidence sufficient to meet this burden when standing is challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of standing determination (standing as of commencement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because standing is determined as of the lawsuit’s commencement, the court must consider the facts as they existed at that time. (Steger v. Franco.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-filing changes (e.g., later termination, assignment, settlement) generally do not cure a lack of standing that existed when the complaint was filed. When evaluating standing, examine the parties' rights and interests as of the date the suit was initiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of assignment/control-of-litigation provisions on standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractual language granting an assignee the 'exclusive right and complete discretion to bring (or not to bring) infringement or unfair competition proceedings or any other legal proceeding' transfers the cause of action and thereby the standing to prosecute those claims to the assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original plaintiff assigned its litigation rights (expressly relinquished the right to bring suits) before filing, the assignor lacks standing. When contracts grant exclusive litigation control to another entity, courts treat that as relinquishment of the right to sue unless the agreement indicates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract interpretation principles under governing state law (Minnesota)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract interpretation is a question of law; its primary goal is to determine and enforce the intent of the parties. The Court first looks to the plain language of the written contract. When that language is clear and unambiguous, it is not for the Court to rewrite it. (Travertine Corp. v. Lexington-Silverwood.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these principles to determine whether contractual language (e.g., about assignment, control, reversion, remedies on termination) expresses the parties' intent. If language is clear, interpret according to its terms; if ambiguous, other interpretive rules may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and effect of Litigation Control/License clauses granting exclusive authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A Litigation Control Agreement giving one party the 'sole and exclusive authority, control and discretion to direct the strategy and make all material decisions' — including 'make settlement offers, accept settlement offers, reject settlement offers, and otherwise determine whether and on what terms to settle' — vests exclusive litigation and settlement authority in that party and may allocate recovered proceeds to that party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such clauses can (1) transfer practical control over litigation decisions to the assignee, (2) define entitlement to settlement proceeds (including punitive-damage splits), and (3) supersede inconsistent prior agreements. When present and unambiguous, courts enforce those powers as written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversion of litigation rights upon termination requires explicit language
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent any language in the agreements indicating an intent to revert litigation rights upon termination, termination does not operate to revert those rights to the original parties; silence on reversion indicates no manifestation of intent to restore litigation rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a party claims rights reverted after termination, the court looks for express contractual language providing for reversion. Termination provisions that address remedies, events upon termination, confidentiality, marketing, and performance do not imply reversion of assigned litigation rights unless stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance (or irrelevance) of notice to defendants about inter-party disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is no indication that plaintiffs conveyed notice of inter-party disputes (e.g., breaches between assignor and assignee) to defendants, defendants and the court may treat the settlement/dismissal as an arm’s-length resolution between adverse parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of notice to defendants supports the court's view that the matter was concluded between the adverse parties in good faith; such background facts may inform equitable assessments but do not alone alter standing or contract rights.
